title: Nucleus: Discovery of Nucleus
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Finding the Needle in the Atom

Thomson's "plum pudding" atom filled space with positive charge. Rutherford's gold-foil experiment blew it apart: nearly all the mass and all the positive charge sit in a tiny, dense **nucleus** — an object 10⁻¹⁵ m across holding 99.9% of the atom's mass.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Rutherford's scattering experiment (1911)

α-particles (helium nuclei) were fired at a thin gold foil (~10⁻⁷ m, a few hundred atoms thick):
- **Most passed straight through** — the atom is mostly empty space.
- **A few deflected by large angles (>90°)** — some encountered a small, massive, positively charged core.

Rutherford concluded: a tiny **nucleus** (radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m vs atomic radius ~10⁻¹⁰ m) contains all positive charge and nearly all mass; electrons orbit far outside.

### 2.2 Nuclear composition

- **Protons:** charge +e, mass 1.673×10⁻²⁷ kg; number = atomic number Z.
- **Neutrons:** charge 0, mass 1.675×10⁻²⁷ kg; number N = A − Z, where A is the mass number.
- **Nucleons** = protons + neutrons (A of them). Nuclear charge = +Ze.

### 2.3 Nuclear properties

- **Nuclear density** is enormous (~2×10¹⁷ kg/m³) and roughly **constant for all nuclei** — mass ∝ volume.
- Nuclear forces bind nucleons against electrical repulsion — short-range, strongly attractive.

### 2.4 Worked numerical

**Q (NEB-style):** Estimate the density of nuclear matter, taking a nucleon's mass as 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg and the nuclear radius as R = 1.2×10⁻¹⁵ A^(1/3) m for A = 1.
$$\rho = \frac{Am_n}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} = \frac{1.67\times10^{-27}}{\frac{4}{3}\pi(1.2\times10^{-15})^3} ≈ 2.3\times10^{17} \text{ kg/m}^3$$
— a teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh ~a billion tonnes.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 106:** density's constancy follows from R ∝ A^(1/3).
- **To Topic 107:** A and Z label isotopes — same Z, different A.
- **To Topic 109:** nuclear forces explain the binding energy.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise the Rutherford conclusions and the nuclear-density estimate as **NEB-style practice** (2–3m).

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. Describe Rutherford's experiment and its conclusions (3–4m).
2. Why is most of the atom empty space? (2m)
3. Nuclear density estimate (3m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Saying α-particles were "reflected by electrons" — electrons are far too light.
2. Confusing atomic (10⁻¹⁰ m) with nuclear (10⁻¹⁵ m) dimensions — a factor of 10⁵.
3. Omitting the observation-to-inference chain in the experiment description.
specificConditions: Alpha Particle Source: Rutherford used alpha particles (helium nuclei, +2e charge, ~5 MeV energy) from radioactive decay (radium/polonium).
Thin Foil: Gold foil used because gold is highly malleable — can be made extremely thin (~400 atoms thick) so alpha particles interact with at most one atom.
Point Charge Approximation: Alpha particle treated as point charge; nucleus treated as point charge — valid since distances are much larger than nuclear/alpha sizes.

summary: Rutherford fired α-particles at thin gold foil: most passed undeflected (the atom is mostly empty space), but ~1 in 8000 suffered large-angle deflections — impossible unless a tiny, massive, positive **nucleus** concentrated the charge and mass. The nucleus (R ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m, vs atom 10⁻¹⁰ m) holds Z protons and N = A − Z neutrons, bound by the short-range strong nuclear force. Its radius scales as R = 1.2A^(1/3) fm, so mass ∝ volume and **nuclear density ≈ 2×10¹⁷ kg/m³** — constant for all nuclei, denser than any everyday matter by a factor of 10¹⁴.

subtopics.name: Rutherford's gold foil experiment
points: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil, 1911
Most passed straight through, some deflected sharply, a few bounced back
Conclusion: positive charge and nearly all mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus

subtopics.name: Earlier discoveries
points: Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 (cathode rays)
Goldstein discovered the proton in 1886 (canal rays)

subtopics.name: Composition and notation
points: Nucleus contains protons (Z) and neutrons (N); mass number A = Z + N
Notation: A over Z before the element symbol
Isotopes have the same Z but different N

subtopics.name: Size and density
points: Nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3), with R0 about 1.2 x 10^-15 m
Nuclear density is roughly constant across all nuclei, about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m^3
The nucleus is about 10^5 times smaller than the atom but holds almost all its mass

subtopics.name: Nuclear forces
points: Strong nuclear force binds nucleons, is short-ranged and charge-independent
It is strongly attractive at about 1-2 fm and repulsive at very short range
Competes with electrostatic repulsion between protons, which limits nucleus size

subtopics.name: Why heavy nuclei are unstable
points: Coulomb repulsion grows as Z^2 while the strong force grows only as A
Beyond bismuth (Z = 83) no stable nucleus exists
Explains alpha decay and spontaneous fission in heavy elements
